prediction_scored: miss: the elasticity is -0.30 (-0.38 to -0.21), negative with an interval that excludes 0, so the registered refute_if is met. The direction is the complement pattern of Barajas and Brown (2021).
settle: The substitution hypothesis is about residents' trips, and zone pickups mix residents with visitors. Trip records linked to the rider's home (or a travel survey such as the NYC Citywide Mobility Survey with household car ownership and distance to the subway) would separate two explanations: that app trips are rarer far from the subway because households there own cars, or that they are rarer because app trips are mostly made in dense, mixed-use areas whatever the subway access. The no-vehicle sensitivity points to the first, but it was not the registered test.

notes:
Sample: 174 taxi zones in the Bronx, Brooklyn, Queens and Staten Island (175 met the population rule; Rikers Island dropped because it has no household income). In 2024 TLC recorded 239.5 million app pickups, 40.6 million yellow taxi pickups and 0.66 million green taxi pickups (c5iv-bn4s). The median zone outside Manhattan had 17.2 app pickups per resident and a population-weighted distance of 0.61 km to a station. Registered sensitivities: unadjusted -0.40 (-0.54 to -0.26); borough fixed effects -0.17 (-0.26 to -0.08); drop-offs -0.31 (-0.39 to -0.24); all boroughs -0.34 (-0.41 to -0.27); yellow and green taxis -0.65 (-0.88 to -0.42). Adding the share of households with no vehicle reverses the sign: +0.14 (+0.04 to +0.25), with each point of no-vehicle share adding 2.8% (log points x 100) to pickups per resident. Distance and no-vehicle share are correlated at -0.76 across zones, so this model rests on the zones where the two diverge. Within boroughs: Bronx -0.08 (-0.20 to +0.04), Brooklyn -0.16 (-0.40 to +0.09), Queens -0.19 (-0.32 to -0.06), Staten Island +0.18 (+0.00 to +0.35). A first run treated Census annotation codes (negative income values) as numbers; they are now set to missing, which changed the primary estimate from -0.29 to -0.30 and restored 11 zones.

After the referee: 'contested' follows the registered rule, but it contradicts the registrant's prediction, not the published research. The one peer-reviewed source (Barajas and Brown 2021) also finds more ride-hail use near transit, and the city data agree with it. The stance is therefore drawn against the research direction. The reversal after adding car-free households is not decisive: car ownership is plausibly a mediator, the reversed estimate is +0.09 with an interval including zero when Staten Island is dropped, and it was registered as report-only.
